resources.string: A free alternative to the paid eloquence text to speech engine.
It is provided free of charge, to break the barrier of paying for a screen reader voice.
It is an all in one replacement for the paid eloquence TTS: eight voices, every setting a voice has, and your own pronunciation dictionaries.

The next screen asks for two permissions: notifications, and an exemption from battery optimization. The exemption is required, because without it Android puts the engine to sleep and the voice stops while the phone is idle.
You can read about the app and its developers at any time from the main screen.
A free alternative to the paid eloquence text to speech engine.
Customize eloquence settings for a robust experience of text to speech.
Open the system text to speech settings and choose your preferred engine there.
Open system text to speech settings
Read about the app and its developers.
Nothing on this device opens the system text to speech settings.

Alt eloquence TTS is the voice of your screen reader, and Android stops an app it counts as using too much power in the background. Allowing the exemption keeps the voice working at all times, including on the lock screen. Choose Allow now, and then allow it on the system screen that opens.
Alt eloquence TTS is not the default engine
Choose Alt eloquence TTS as your preferred text to speech engine in the system settings, for a robust voice that is always available.
Open system text to speech settings
Select a voice variant and set the gender.
Speak at the rate set here even when another app, such as TalkBack, asks for a different one.
Speak at the pitch set here even when another app, such as TalkBack, asks for a different one.
Speak at the volume set here even when another app, such as TalkBack, asks for a different one.
Customize the voice inflection, which is how far the pitch rises and falls across a sentence.
Customize the voice breathiness, which is how much breath is heard in it.
Customize the voice head size, which is how large the head speaking it is, and so how much it resonates.
Customize the voice roughness, which is how rough or how smooth it sounds.
The rate the speech is made at. A higher one is clearer and costs more power.
Teach the engine the words it would otherwise spell out, letter by letter.
A list of your own words and what to say instead. Add words one at a time, or bring a whole file in.
Each word is read as you wrote it, and then as the engine will say it. Tap a word to edit it or take it away, and use Add word to teach a new one.
No words yet. Add one, or import a dictionary file.
What to do with this word?
Nothing in that file could be read as dictionary words.
The dictionary could not be written to that file.
Reads an abbreviation as the words it stands for. Off by default, because it expands whatever it takes for an abbreviation whether that was wanted or not.
How a run of digits is read. Choose digits for one at a time, pairs for two at a time, triplets for three, or leave the numbers to the engine.
Says an emoji by its name, such as smiling face for a smile, and turns a typed emoticon into its name too. Off, an emoji is a gap, the way the engine has always left it.
What a capital letter standing on its own is said as. It only touches a letter with nothing beside it, so words and lines of capitals are left alone.
Takes SSML and other tags out of the text before it is read, so a tag is never spoken. The words between tags are kept.
Lets the engine shape the intonation of a phrase and pause where the phrase ends. Off, it pauses only at punctuation, which suits a screen reader that reads a fragment at a time.
Everything this app can do to keep Android from stopping the voice in the background.
The exemption from battery optimization, a persistent notification, a wake lock while speaking, and a log of your actions.
A screen reader is the last thing that can be allowed to sleep. Each of these makes Android a little more likely to leave the engine running, at a small cost in battery or in noise.
Not granted. Tap to allow it.
The one setting that matters most. Without the exemption Android puts the engine to sleep when the phone is idle, and the voice stops. Tap to open the system screen that grants it.

Keeps a notification showing while the engine is in use, which holds it in the foreground where Android does not kill it. The app checks every few seconds that the notification is still there and restores it if it is not.
Keep the CPU awake while speaking
Holds the processor awake while an utterance is being made. On some devices the CPU sleeps mid sentence and the tail of the speech is lost.
Writes what you do on this screen to the system log, so a problem with the engine stopping can be traced back to what was changed.
The engine stays in the foreground so the voice keeps working in the background.
Eloquence pauses generously, which reads well in prose and slowly in a screen reader, where most of what is read is a few words.
How much of the punctuation and the other symbols in the text is spoken by name.
Every symbol is spoken by name, including periods and commas.
Brackets, quotes, question marks and the like are spoken as well.
Currency and math symbols are spoken, and a symbol standing on its own is always named.
Only the symbols you enter are spoken by name.
No symbol is spoken by name.
Enter the symbols that should be pronounced
Reset this voice to its defaults
%1$s is back to the settings it shipped with.
Forgets what has been changed for the voice chosen above. Every other voice is left alone, and so is the rate, which is yours rather than the voice\'s.
Nothing here speaks by itself. Every setting is in force the moment it is changed, and this is how you hear the result.
Alt eloquence TTS is a free eloquence text to speech engine for Android and for Wear OS.
It is built for blind and low vision people. Every control on every screen is one stop for a screen reader, says what it is and what it is set to, and can be changed without leaving the screen.

It is free, and it asks for no account, no payment and nothing from the network. The two permissions it asks for are notifications and an exemption from battery optimization, and both are about staying available while the phone is idle.
It is a hobby project, and nobody\'s product. It is not from IBM, Nuance, Cerence or Google, and none of them have endorsed or reviewed it.
Developed by Sujan Rai, with the Blind Tech Nexus team.
